records.description: Same brand, IDENTICAL marketing title, two different retailers, two different colorways (carried only in the variant field, which the title text does not mention). canonicalProductKey reads only brand+title, never variant/color, so this is EXACTLY the shape of listing the real, dormant algorithm would collapse together -- and exactly the shape the corpus's doctrine requires stay separate absent an exact identity match.
records.notes: Directly models supabase/functions/scan-identify/canonicalCommerce.ts:133-141 canonicalProductKey's real, EMPIRICALLY VERIFIED behavior (see __tests__/commerce-corpus/groupingDoctrine.test.js, which calls the real function on this exact fixture): the key is computed from brand + up-to-8 normalized title TOKENS only -- it never reads `variant`/`color` -- so two colorways sharing one marketing title produce the IDENTICAL key. A merely 'similar but not identical' title (e.g. one listing adding a size word or reordering words) does NOT reliably collide, because titleIdentityTokens() compares the full sorted token SET; this fixture uses the realistic colorway-collision shape the algorithm's own author flagged as risky in supabase/functions/scan-identify/watchlistCapability.ts:9-11 ('groups colorways together and is unstable under a retailer re-title'). This is Finding F2's central evidence.

records.description: Two listings sharing the exact same product photo but different SKU/productId values must stay separate — a shared stock photo is not proof of shared identity (retailers frequently reuse manufacturer stock photography across different variants or even different products).
Same brand and same color description is still not enough to prove identity — many products from one brand share both.

A one-character title typo between two listings (e.g. a transposed letter) must not be treated as proof they are the same listing at two retailers — a fuzzy/edit-distance match is exactly the kind of implicit identity this corpus forbids.
Two entirely different products in the same category (e.g. two different sneakers) must never be grouped merely for sharing a category.
Two listings from the SAME retailer with similar names must still stay separate absent an exact ID match — same-retailer proximity is not identity either.
Visual/perceptual image similarity alone (no shared exact identity field at all) must never license grouping — this corpus does not endorse an image-hash-based matching heuristic as identity.
Two products in the same model family (e.g. two different generations/versions of the same sneaker line) must not be grouped as the same product.
Two visually similar but genuinely different garments from different brands must never be grouped just because they look alike in a photo.
